title: Cities of the World
description: Ten portraits of cities: Lisbon's trams and hills, Mexico City on its lost lake, Istanbul between two continents, Singapore's gardens, Montreal in two languages, Nairobi's growth, Venice and the tides, Seoul's restored stream, Marie Curie's Paris and Cape Town under its mountain.

lessons.title: Lisbon, One Hill at a Time
lessons.summary: A visitor rides Lisbon's old trams up its hills, listens to fado and thinks about the city's writers.
lessons.text:
Lisbon is a city that makes you earn its views. It rises from the wide mouth of the Tagus River across seven hills, and almost every walk in the old districts, sooner or later, turns upward. On my first morning, I decided to let the city's oldest trams do the climbing for me.

The number 28 tram is small, yellow and largely made of wood, and some of its cars were first built almost a century ago. It climbs upward through streets so narrow that I could almost touch the walls, and on the steepest corners it seems to tug itself up the hill by will alone. The driver handled it proudly, the way a fisherman handles an old boat, ringing the bell at every blind corner. Asked whether the tram ever broke down, he said proudly that it was older than his grandfather and more reliable.

From the top of the Graça hill, I could see red roofs, white towers and the wide river. In the afternoon, the sun bounced off the water and the pale stones of the streets with a glare that sent me looking for my sunglasses. Even the sidewalks, made of small white and black stones laid by hand in waves and stars, throw back a hard glare at noon.

Lisbon also has a moody side. When fog rolls in from the Atlantic, the hills vanish one by one, the river turns gray, and the city seems lost in its own thoughts. That moody weather suits the music of Lisbon, which is called fado.

In the evening, I went to a small fado house in Alfama, the oldest district. Fado needs only a singer, usually dressed in black, and two guitarists. One guitarist plays an ordinary guitar; the other plays the Portuguese guitar, a rounded instrument with twelve strings and a bright, ringing voice. Before the first song, the lights were dimmed and the waiter asked for silence. Audiences are expected to be respectful: no talking, not even a whisper, while the singer sings. It was the most respectful silence I have ever heard.

The songs are about longing, the sea, lost love and sometimes betrayal: a lover who left, a promise that was broken. I understood few of the words, yet the music tugged at my heart all the same. After a song about betrayal, the older guitarist nodded at the young singer, as if to tell her that she had done the song justice.

Lisbon has also shaped many writers. The acclaimed novelist José Saramago, who won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1998, spent much of his life here. He did not become widely known until he was about sixty. Novelists, I thought as I walked home, are a little like this city: what they give you is rarely obvious at first, and you have to climb for it.

Questions:
Why does almost every walk in old Lisbon turn upward?
The city rises across seven hills, so the streets climb from the river.
What did the driver say proudly about his tram?
He said that it was older than his grandfather and more reliable.
Why did the writer need sunglasses?
The sun bounced off the river and the pale stones with a strong glare.
How are audiences expected to behave in a fado house?
They are expected to be respectful and silent while the singer sings.
Who was José Saramago?
He was an acclaimed novelist who won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1998.

lessons.title: Mexico City, the Lake Beneath the Streets
lessons.summary: An essay on how Mexico City grew from an island city in a lake, and how the lost lake still shapes it.
lessons.text:
When Spanish soldiers first saw the capital of the Mexica in 1519, they compared it to a dream. The city of Tenochtitlan stood on an island in Lake Texcoco, linked to the shore by long roads built across the water. Today it is Mexico City, one of the largest cities in the world, and although the lake has almost disappeared, it still shapes the city.

The Mexica founded their city in 1325, and within two centuries their domination stretched across much of central Mexico. That domination rested on war, but also on food, which the Mexica grew in a clever way. In the shallow parts of the lake, farmers built chinampas, long, narrow fields made of layers of mud and plants. The soil was rich and wet, so farmers could reap several harvests a year. They reaped corn, beans, squash and chilies, the dietary base of the region, and those dietary habits live on today.

Keeping such a field alive was a daily chore. Farmers scooped fresh mud from the bottom of the canals and spread it over their fields, a chore that kept the soil rich and the canals deep. In Xochimilco, in the south of the city, some families still farm this way. Early each morning, they load crates of vegetables and flowers onto flat boats, and the crates travel along the canals to market, as they have for centuries.

After the Spanish conquest in 1521, the new rulers saw the lake as an enemy, because floods came again and again. Over the following centuries, engineers drained it.

Draining the lake solved one problem and created another. The city stands on soft clay, the old bed of the lake, and it pumps much of its water from under the ground. As the water is removed, the clay shrinks, and the city sinks, in some districts by more than a foot a year. Streets and sidewalks buckle, pipes crack and old churches lean. The great cathedral on the main square sank so badly on one side that engineers had to dig carefully beneath it so that it would settle more evenly. Experts agree that it is imperative to take less water from under the city and to collect more rain. It is just as imperative to repair old pipes that leak.

The soft clay has another effect: in an earthquake, it shakes like jelly. For that reason, the city has an early warning system. Sensors along the Pacific coast, where many large earthquakes begin, detect the first movement, and a transmitter sends a radio signal to the city. Because radio waves travel far faster than the shaking, the signal can arrive up to a minute early, and sirens across the city begin to sound. Every transmitter is checked routinely, and the people of the city routinely take part in national drills.

The lake is gone, yet it is everywhere, even in the warning that sounds before the ground moves.

Questions:
Where did the city of Tenochtitlan stand?
It stood on an island in Lake Texcoco.
Why could farmers reap several harvests a year?
The soil of their fields was rich and always wet.
What daily chore kept the fields alive?
Farmers scooped fresh mud from the canals and spread it over their fields.
What happens as the city sinks?
Streets and sidewalks buckle, pipes crack and old churches lean.
How does the transmitter help people before an earthquake?
It sends a radio signal from the coast, which can arrive up to a minute before the shaking.

lessons.title: Istanbul, a Seam Between Two Continents
lessons.summary: A visitor crosses the Bosphorus by ferry and explores the old markets of Istanbul.
lessons.text:
Few cities sit on two continents, and none is as famous for it as Istanbul. The city lies on both sides of the Bosphorus, a narrow strait that joins the Black Sea to the Sea of Marmara and divides Europe from Asia. On a map, the Bosphorus looks like a line that cuts the city in two. After a week there, I came to see it differently: not as a cut but as a seam, the line where two pieces of cloth are stitched together.

The best place to see the seam is the deck of a ferry. For the price of a bus ticket, you can cross from Europe to Asia in about twenty minutes. A cloud of white birds follows the boat. Passengers throw them pieces of bread, and the birds catch every piece while still airborne. One bird stayed airborne beside my window for the whole crossing, as if it had bought a ticket too.

People here like to argue about which side of the city is better. The answer, a woman beside me said, depends on whichever side you happen to live on. She lived in Asia, worked in Europe and loved the fact that, whichever shore she was on, the other was always in sight.

For about sixteen centuries, the city was the capital of great empires, first as Constantinople and later as Istanbul. Because it controlled the passage between two seas and the roads between two continents, it became a great mart, a place where silk, spices, gold and ideas changed hands. Something of the old mart survives in the Grand Bazaar, one of the oldest covered markets in the world. Its heavy gates are still locked every night, as they were centuries ago, when guards kept robbers away from the stalls of gold and silk. A seller told me, with a laugh, that the only robbers left in the bazaar were the cats that try to steal his lunch.

Down by the water stands the Spice Bazaar, which smells exactly as its name promises. There were sacks of red pepper and bundles of cinnamon sticks tied with string. I bought a bag of cinnamon for my mother. In a small shop nearby, an old man offered me a drop of rose attar, an oil made from roses. It takes thousands of flowers to fill one small bottle, he explained, which is why good attar has always been precious.

A careful shopper soon learns that, in these markets, the first price is a beginning, not an end. Bargaining is expected, but it is a polite ritual, and a patient shopper usually leaves with a fair price and a good story.

On my last evening, as I crossed the water once more, the lights of both shores came on, and the seam between the continents shone like gold thread.

Questions:
Why did the writer come to see the Bosphorus as a seam?
It joins the two halves of the city, like a seam in cloth.
What did the birds do while they were airborne?
They caught the pieces of bread that passengers threw to them.
Which side of the city is better, according to the woman on the ferry?
It depends on whichever side you happen to live on.
Why did the city become a great mart?
It controlled the passage between two seas and the roads between two continents.
What is attar?
It is an oil made from roses.

lessons.title: Singapore, a City in a Garden
lessons.summary: A portrait of Singapore's gardens, orchids, food and streets in a city where it is summer all year.
lessons.text:
Singapore is a small island nation close to the equator, where the temperature hardly changes all year. Words like winter and autumn are almost meaningless here. Every day is warm and wet, and many afternoons end in a short, heavy storm. A forecast that promises a hot day tomorrow is just as meaningless, since every day is hot.

For a crowded city of almost six million people, Singapore is surprisingly green, and that is no accident. In 1967, the country's first prime minister set out a plan to turn Singapore into a garden city, and millions of trees were later planted along its roads.

The oldest of its gardens is the Botanic Gardens, founded in 1859 and named a World Heritage Site in 2015. Inside it lies the National Orchid Garden, where breeders have created more than 2,000 new kinds of orchid by crossing different plants. A breeder needs great patience, because a seed may take years to grow into a plant that flowers. If the chromosomes of the two parent plants are too different, the seeds may never grow, so breeders keep careful records of each plant and its chromosome count. The results vary wildly. Some flowers are no bigger than a button; others are as large as a hand, in colors that range wildly from snow white to deep purple.

A newer garden, Gardens by the Bay, opened in 2012 on land taken from the sea. Its most famous sights are the Supertrees, giant steel towers up to 50 meters tall, covered in living plants. Every evening, music plays and thousands of lights seem to ignite the towers, which glow in changing colors. It looks as if someone has managed to ignite a forest without burning a single leaf.

The city has also been responsive to its climate. Many new buildings are expected to replace the green space they take up with gardens on their roofs and walls, which cool the air. Planners who are responsive to the heat also cover many walking paths with roofs against both sun and rain.

Then there is the food. In the hawker centers, large open halls full of small food stalls, a family can eat well for a few dollars. Noodles are everywhere: fried flat noodles with egg and shrimp, or thin noodles in a spicy coconut soup. Breakfast is often toast spread with a sweet coconut jam, which people dunk into soft eggs mixed with a little dark sauce, or dunk into a cup of strong, sweet coffee.

Singapore's mix of peoples shows on its streets as well. On a single short street in the old center, a temple, a mosque, a shrine and a Methodist church stand within a few minutes' walk of one another. The Methodist church is about a hundred years old, and its members share the street, the storms and the heat with everyone else.

Questions:
Why are words like winter almost meaningless in Singapore?
The temperature hardly changes, and every day is warm and wet.
Why does an orchid breeder need patience?
A seed may take years to grow into a plant that flowers.
What can happen if the chromosomes of two parent plants are too different?
The seeds may never grow.
What happens to the Supertrees every evening?
Music plays and thousands of lights seem to ignite the towers.
What do people dunk their toast into at breakfast?
They dunk it into soft eggs with dark sauce or into strong, sweet coffee.

lessons.title: Montreal, a Winter in Two Languages
lessons.summary: A student from Ohio spends a winter in Montreal, learning French, eating bagels and going to hockey games.
lessons.text:
When I arrived in Montreal from Ohio to study for a year, I thought I spoke some French. My first morning in a café proved otherwise. I tried to order coffee and a roll in French and made a complete hash of it: wrong words, wrong order and a terrible accent. The young man behind the counter smiled kindly and answered in perfect English. I promised myself that I would not make such a hash of things again.

Montreal is one of the great linguistic meeting places of the world. It is the largest city in Quebec, where French is the only official language, but many of its people move between French and English all day without thinking. To a student of languages, the whole city feels like a linguistic laboratory.

French is not optional here. Since 1977, a law has protected the place of the language in public life. For most children, going to school in French is compulsory, and even in English schools, French classes are compulsory from an early age.

In French, every noun is masculine or feminine. The word for subway is masculine; the word for snow is feminine. The girl next door, who was seven, decided to help me. Every morning on the stairs she made me recite ten nouns with their genders, and she recited them with me when I got stuck. By February I could recite fifty.

Winter in Montreal is serious. In January, the temperature can fall below minus four degrees Fahrenheit, and my apartment's old heater clicked and knocked all night. When the heater broke one morning, the building manager fixed it within an hour, because in this city a broken heater is an emergency. After every storm, people came out with a shovel to clear their steps, and I bought a shovel of my own in the second week.

The cold was easier to bear with a warm bagel. Montreal bagels are smaller and sweeter than the ones I knew at home. The dough, made with yeast, egg and a little honey, is boiled in honey water and baked in a wood oven. Late one night, I watched a baker mix yeast and flour while snow fell outside the window.

On weekends I went to hockey games. The city's professional hockey team has a mascot called Youppi, a large orange creature who dances in the stands, and children love the mascot as much as the players. I also watched our university's varsity team. Hockey has deep roots here: one of the first organized indoor games was played in Montreal in 1875, with university students among the players. At every varsity game, I felt part of that long history.

In summer, my friends told me, people paddle small boats along the old canal near the river. I plan to come back, paddle along that canal and order my coffee in good French.

Questions:
What happened when the writer first ordered coffee in French?
The writer made a complete hash of it, and the young man answered in English.
Why does the city feel like a linguistic laboratory?
Many of its people move between French and English all day.
How did the girl next door help the writer?
She made the writer recite ten nouns with their genders every morning.
What is a Montreal bagel made with?
The dough is made with yeast, egg and a little honey, and it is boiled in honey water.

lessons.title: Nairobi, the Place of Cool Water
lessons.summary: A portrait of Nairobi: its railway beginnings, its fast growth, its mobile money and the wild park at its edge.
lessons.text:
Nairobi is a young city. In 1899, the builders of a railway from the port of Mombasa to Lake Victoria set up a supply camp on a wet, open plain beside a small river. The Maasai, who brought their cattle to drink there, called the place Enkare Nairobi, which means "cool water," and the camp kept the name. The camp soon became a town, and in 1963 it became the capital of independent Kenya. Today more than four million people live in the city.

Like many fast-growing cities, Nairobi was built by people from somewhere else. For many families who left their villages, a respectable job in an office was the measure of success. A respectable job is still a dream for many, but a large share of the city's people now work for themselves, selling fruit, repairing phones or driving taxis.

For these small businesses, one invention changed everything. In 2007, a phone company launched a service called M-Pesa, which lets people send and receive money by text message. Even people without a bank account can be paid in seconds. Each payment goes through verification: the person paying types a secret number to authorize it, and both people receive a message confirming the amount. This simple verification has made the system widely trusted.

The buses themselves are a sight. Nairobi's matatus, the small private buses that carry many of the city's passengers, are often painted with bright pictures and play loud music. The most stylish ones have glowing lights and screens inside, and young passengers sometimes choose a bus because it is the most stylish on the road. In the city's hair salons, women braid hair into fine, careful patterns. Braiding a full head of hair can take a whole afternoon, so the salon becomes a place to share news.

At the city's southern edge lies Nairobi National Park, founded in 1946 as the country's first national park. Lions, rhinos and buffalo live there, only a few miles from the center, with office towers behind them. A fence runs along the perimeter of the park on the sides that face the city, but the southern side of the perimeter is left open, so that wild animals can move to and from the plains beyond.

In the grass stand tall, hard mounds built by termites. Each mound is a city of its own, where every insect belongs to a caste with its own work: workers build and feed, soldiers defend, and a single queen lays eggs. No insect changes its caste. The queen's abdomen, full of eggs, grows so large that she can no longer move, and she may lay thousands of eggs a day.

An hour's drive northwest of the city, the land suddenly drops away into the Great Rift Valley, a vast crack in the earth's surface where the continent is very slowly pulling apart. Standing at the edge of the rift, a visitor feels how young the city is beside it.

Questions:
How does a person authorize a payment with M-Pesa?
The person types a secret number.
What is special about the perimeter of the national park?
It is fenced on the sides that face the city, but the southern side is open for wild animals.
What happens to the abdomen of a termite queen?
It grows so large that she can no longer move.
What is the Great Rift Valley?
It is a vast crack in the earth's surface where the continent is slowly pulling apart.

lessons.title: Venice and the Tides
lessons.summary: A young couple on their honeymoon in Venice see the city flood with the tide and learn how it protects itself.
lessons.text:
Lucy and Daniel chose Venice for their honeymoon. They arrived in early November, when the summer crowds had gone. On their first evening, they walked for an hour without hearing a single car. Venice has no roads for cars, only canals and narrow stone streets, and the only sound was their own footsteps. Each footstep echoed from the walls, and Lucy said that she had never heard her footsteps so clearly.

Their hotel was run by a woman named Elena, whose family had lived in Venice for generations. On the second morning, she gave them a card with the times of the tides. Venice sits in a shallow, tidal bay of the Adriatic Sea, and twice a day the water rises and falls. In late autumn, when strong winds push water from the sea into the bay, the tidal rise can flood the lowest parts of the city.

That afternoon, a siren sounded across the city, followed by a series of musical tones. Elena explained that the more tones there are, the higher the water will come. Within an hour, St. Mark's Square, the lowest part of the city, began to fill. Lucy expected the canals to overflow their banks, but the water came up through the drains in the square. The canals do overflow in a very high tide, Elena said, but the first water usually rises from beneath.

Workers set up raised wooden paths, and people walked in single file above the water. A few visitors who had not checked the tides were stranded in a café. A waiter brought them coffee, gave Daniel a wink and said that the water would be gone by dinner. He was right. The tide fell, and the stranded visitors walked out in borrowed boots, while the waiter gave Lucy a wink as well.

That evening, Elena told them about the grim night of November 12, 2019, when the water rose higher than at any time in more than fifty years. Boats were thrown onto the streets, shops were ruined, and the floor of the great cathedral was under water. It was a grim time, she said, and many families lost things that could never be replaced.

Since 2020, the city has had a new defense: a line of 78 steel gates at the three openings between the bay and the sea. When a dangerous tide is forecast, the gates rise from the sea floor and hold the water back. Elena was quick to scotch a common rumor: the gates do not stay closed all winter, but rise only when a very high tide is coming. She has had to scotch the same rumor for many guests. Smaller tides still flood the square, she added, and the sea itself is slowly rising.

On their last morning, Lucy and Daniel walked to the square again. They listened to their footsteps on the stones and agreed that it had been the perfect honeymoon.

Questions:
Why did Lucy and Daniel hear their footsteps so clearly?
Venice has no roads for cars, so there was almost no other sound.
What do the musical tones after the siren mean?
The more tones there are, the higher the water will come.
What happened to the stranded visitors in the café?
They walked out in borrowed boots when the tide fell.
What rumor did Elena scotch?
She said that the gates do not stay closed all winter.

lessons.title: Seoul and the Stream That Came Back
lessons.summary: An essay on how Seoul removed a highway and brought back a stream in its city center, and what people think of it.
lessons.text:
For six centuries, a stream ran through the heart of Seoul. It was called Cheonggyecheon, and in the days of the old kings it carried rain out of the city and gave women a place to wash clothes. As the city grew in the twentieth century, the stream became a problem. Houses crowded its banks, waste ran into it, and the contamination grew so bad that the water smelled from far away. In the rainy season, the rising water seemed to dilute the waste, but rain could dilute it only for a few weeks, and every dry season the smell returned.

The city's answer was to bury the stream. After the war, it was covered with concrete, and by 1971 a raised highway ran on top of it. For a generation, this was a symbol of progress. It was also dark, ugly and noisy. Day and night, the noisy traffic overhead never stopped.

In 2003, the city did something that few cities had tried: it pulled down the highway and opened the stream again. Thousands of shop owners worked in the area, and many were unwilling to move or to lose customers during the work. City officials held thousands of meetings with them, and many who had been unwilling at first eventually agreed. In 2005, a clean stream with paths, bridges and stepping stones flowed again through the center of Seoul.

People came at once, and the stream became a place for spontaneous meetings: office workers ate lunch on the stones, and children took off their shoes and stepped into the water. Nobody organizes this life; it is entirely spontaneous. Fish, birds and insects returned. Unexpectedly, the area also became cooler: on hot summer days, the air along the stream is several degrees cooler than on a busy road nearby. And, unexpectedly for many drivers, traffic in the center did not become worse, partly because the city improved its buses.

The stream also hosts a recurring event. Every November, a lantern festival fills the water with glowing lanterns. Many lanterns are covered with traditional Korean paper, made from the pulp of tree bark. The pulp is beaten, spread thin and dried, and the paper it produces is strong and lets light through softly. For many visitors, the lanterns evoke the old city that disappeared under the concrete, and the festival has become one of the most popular recurring events in Seoul.

Not everyone is satisfied. Critics point out that the stream is not truly natural: most of its water is pumped from a large river and from underground, and it costs a great deal to run. They say it can evoke nature but not replace it. Supporters reply that a city of almost ten million people cannot have a wild river in its center, and that a clean, living stream is far better than a dark and noisy highway. Both views contain some truth.

Questions:
Why did the stream become a problem in the twentieth century?
Waste ran into it, and the contamination grew so bad that the water smelled from far away.
What happened unexpectedly after the stream was opened?
The area became cooler, and traffic in the center did not become worse.
What is the recurring event on the stream?
Every November, a lantern festival fills the water with glowing lanterns.
What do critics say about the stream?
They say it is not truly natural, because most of its water is pumped.

lessons.title: Marie Curie's Paris
lessons.summary: A profile of Marie Curie, who came to Paris to study, discovered new elements there and changed science.
lessons.text:
In 1891, a young Polish woman named Maria Skłodowska arrived in Paris with a great hunger to learn. In an age when most women were expected to become a housewife and nothing more, she enrolled at the Sorbonne, one of the few universities in Europe that admitted women. She lived in a tiny room and finished first in her class in physics. At home she might have become a teacher or a housewife; Paris allowed her to become a scientist.

There she met Pierre Curie, a quiet scientist who studied crystals, and they married in 1895. Marie Curie began to study the strange rays that uranium gives off. To measure them, she used an instrument that Pierre and his brother had developed, based on a thin piece of quartz. Quartz has a remarkable property: when it is squeezed, it produces a tiny electric charge. With the quartz instrument, Marie could measure rays too weak for any other tool.

Her measurements led her to suspect that certain rocks contained unknown elements. To find them, the couple worked in an old shed with a roof that let in the rain. They processed tons of rock by hand. Marie stirred boiling pots with an iron rod nearly as tall as herself, working manually through every stage, because no machine for the job existed. Working as a chemist, she separated the rock into smaller and smaller parts, and in 1898 the couple announced two new elements: polonium, named after her homeland, and radium.

Other scientists questioned the validity of their claims. To prove the validity of the discovery, Marie spent four more years isolating a tiny amount of radium. In 1903, she and Pierre shared the Nobel Prize in Physics with the scientist Henri Becquerel.

Radium gives off several kinds of rays, including gamma rays, which pass easily through paper, wood and the human body. Gamma rays would later be used to treat disease, but the Curies did not yet understand how dangerous they were, and Pierre sometimes carried a glowing sample in his pocket.

In 1906, Pierre was killed in a street accident. His death was premature and terrible, and Marie was left alone with two daughters. She took over his teaching post and became the first woman to teach at the Sorbonne. In 1911, newspapers hounded her about her private life, yet that same year she won a second Nobel Prize, this time in chemistry. She was the first person to win two. The press had hounded her, but the scientific world honored her as a great chemist.

She died in 1934, probably of an illness caused by the radiation she had worked with for so long. Like Pierre's, her death was premature.

Her papers are still contaminated. Her notebooks, kept in a national library in Paris, will remain radioactive for more than a thousand years. Each contaminated notebook is stored in a box lined with lead, and anyone who wishes to read one must wear protective clothing and sign a waiver accepting the risk. Scholars sign the waiver happily, because few documents tell a more remarkable story.

Questions:
Why did Maria Skłodowska come to Paris?
She came to study at the Sorbonne.
How did Marie Curie process the rock?
She worked manually, stirring boiling pots with an iron rod.
Why did she spend four more years isolating radium?
She wanted to prove the validity of the discovery.
What must a person do before reading one of her notebooks?
The reader must wear protective clothing and sign a waiver accepting the risk.

lessons.title: Cape Town Under the Mountain
lessons.summary: A portrait of Cape Town: its mountain and cloud, its rare plants, its old fort and the first heart transplant.
lessons.text:
Cape Town lies near the southern tip of Africa, between the ocean and a mountain with a flat top. Table Mountain rises more than 3,000 feet behind the city, and on many summer days a white cloud pours over its top and down its sides like a cloth spread on a table. People in Cape Town call it the tablecloth. The cloud can conceal the top of the mountain in minutes, and on some days it seems to conceal half the city as well.

The mountain is home to some of the richest flora on earth. The Cape region has about 9,000 kinds of plants, and most of them grow nowhere else. Much of this flora is fynbos, a low, tough and colorful mix of bushes and flowers that has learned to live with poor soil, strong winds and regular fires.

Walkers on the mountain and along the coast soon see signs that say "Beware of baboons." Baboons are large monkeys that have learned that people carry food. A frightened or hungry baboon can injure a person who tries to take food back, so rangers ask visitors to keep their bags closed. Walkers should also beware of the weather: those who climb when the tablecloth is coming down risk getting lost or injuring themselves on wet rock.

In the city stands the Castle of Good Hope, the oldest surviving colonial building in South Africa. The Dutch built it between 1666 and 1679 in the shape of a pentagon, with five pointed corners. The pentagon shape allowed soldiers on each corner to watch the walls beside it.

Cape Town also has a place in medical history. On December 3, 1967, at Groote Schuur Hospital, a team led by the surgeon Christiaan Barnard performed the first human heart transplant. The donor was a young woman, Denise Darvall, who had died after a road accident. The patient, Louis Washkansky, was a man of 53 with a failing heart. When the new heart was in place, it did not beat at first. An electric shock was needed, and after that stimulation the heart began its first heartbeat in another person's body. Those who were there remembered the room falling silent as the heartbeat grew steady.

Washkansky lived for 18 days. His doctors, his nurses and every caregiver around him worked day and night, but the drugs that stopped his body from attacking the new heart also weakened its defenses, and he died of a lung infection. Real progress came in 1983, when doctors began to use cyclosporine widely. This drug is an inhibitor that calms the body's defenses more precisely. With this inhibitor, many patients began to live for years with a new heart. Today a museum at the hospital tells the story of the operation and of each caregiver who was part of it.

Some of Cape Town's stories, like that first heartbeat in an operating room, belong to the whole world.

Questions:
What is the tablecloth?
It is a white cloud that pours over Table Mountain and can conceal its top in minutes.
What is special about the flora of the Cape region?
It has about 9,000 kinds of plants, and most of them grow nowhere else.
Why do signs tell visitors to beware of baboons?
A frightened or hungry baboon can injure a person who tries to take food back.
What made the new heart start beating?
An electric shock was needed, and after that stimulation the heart began to beat.
